claim: The specificity of TCR:peptide-MHC interactions underlies nearly all adaptive immune responses.
source: The specificity of TCR:peptide-MHC interactions, thus, underlies nearly all adaptive immune responses.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of TCR:pMHC interactions in adaptive immunity.

claim: Two key barriers to generalizable predictive models of TCR:peptide-MHC specificity are the diversity of TCR recognition modes and the paucity of training data.
source: Despite intense interest, generalizable predictive models of TCR:peptide-MHC specificity remain out of reach; two key barriers are the diversity of TCR recognition modes and the paucity of training data.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to the challenges in the field and is based on established understanding of the limitations.

claim: A specialized version of AlphaFold can generate models of TCR:peptide-MHC interactions that can discriminate correct from incorrect peptide epitopes with substantial accuracy.
source: We show that a specialized version of the neural network predictor AlphaFold can generate models of TCR:peptide-MHC interactions that can be used to discriminate correct from incorrect peptide epitopes with substantial accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in the binding specificity prediction section.

claim: Deep learning-based structural modeling represents a path to generalizable prediction of TCR:peptide-MHC interaction specificity.
source: Although much work remains to be done for these predictions to have widespread practical utility, we are optimistic that deep learning-based structural modeling represents a path to generalizable prediction of TCR:peptide-MHC interaction specificity.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Existing predictors can learn to recognize new TCR sequences specific for pMHCs in their training set, but robust generalization to unseen pMHC epitopes has not been convincingly demonstrated.
source: Despite recent progress in TCR sequence analysis and modeling (Gielis et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020; Mayer-Blackwell et al., 2021; Montemurro et al., 2021), a generalizable predictive model of TCR:pMHC interactions remains out of reach: existing predictors can learn to recognize new TCR sequences specific for pMHCs in their training set, but robust generalization to unseen pMHC epitopes has not been convincingly demonstrated (Moris et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Two key difficulties in TCR:pMHC prediction are the diversity of TCR:pMHC recognition modes and the limited number of experimentally validated TCR:pMHC interaction examples for use in training.
source: Two key difficulties are the diversity of TCR:pMHC recognition modes, a consequence of TCR sequence and structural diversity and flexibility in TCR:pMHC docking orientation, and the limited number of experimentally validated TCR:pMHC interaction examples for use in training.
evidence: This statement reflects established challenges in the field based on prior knowledge and literature.

claim: At the biophysical level, TCR:pMHC interaction specificity is determined by the structures and flexibilities of the interacting partners.
source: At the biophysical level, TCR:pMHC interaction specificity is determined by the structures and flexibilities of the interacting partners.
evidence: This is a statement of established biophysical principles.

claim: Experimentally determined TCR:pMHC structures define a range of docking geometries that likely covers the majority of unseen interactions.
source: Collectively, these experimentally determined structures define a range of docking geometries that likely covers the majority of unseen interactions; they also provide valuable templates for cutting-edge deep neural network structure prediction methods such as AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021) and RoseTTAfold (Baek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the body of structural studies and is supported by citations.

claim: AlphaFold and RoseTTAfold feature advanced network architectures with millions of parameters that are trained on structurally characterized proteins and their sequence homologs.
source: These prediction tools feature advanced network architectures with millions of parameters that are trained on structurally characterized proteins and their sequence homologs.
evidence: This is a description of the AlphaFold and RoseTTAfold methods, supported by citations.

claim: AlphaFold and RoseTTAfold can generate state-of-the-art structure predictions for protein complexes despite being trained on monomeric structures.
source: Despite being trained on monomeric structures, these approaches can generate state-of-the-art structure predictions for protein complexes, and they have even been used to predict whether or not protein pairs will associate (Humphreys et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The default AlphaFold version trained to predict protein:protein docking (AlphaFold-Multimer) shows inconsistent performance on TCR:pMHC structures.
source: Whereas the default AlphaFold version trained to predict protein:protein docking (AlphaFold-Multimer Evans et al., 2021) shows inconsistent performance on TCR:pMHC structures (Yin et al., 2022), our specialized pipeline demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced computational cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The specialized AlphaFold pipeline demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced computational cost compared to AlphaFold-Multimer.
source: Whereas the default AlphaFold version trained to predict protein:protein docking (AlphaFold-Multimer Evans et al., 2021) shows inconsistent performance on TCR:pMHC structures (Yin et al., 2022), our specialized pipeline demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced computational cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 2.

claim: The modeling pipeline has significant power to discriminate target peptides from decoy peptides as evaluated on a benchmark of human and mouse MHC class I epitopes.
source: Moreover, this modeling pipeline has significant power to discriminate target peptides from decoy peptides as evaluated on a benchmark of human and mouse MHC class I epitopes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the binding specificity prediction section.

claim: Success in predicting the correct peptide target correlates with structural accuracy of the models.
source: Importantly, success in predicting the correct peptide target correlates with structural accuracy of the models, suggesting that when the pipeline succeeds, it does so by recapitulating key specificity determinants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: When the pipeline succeeds in predicting the correct peptide, it does so by recapitulating key specificity determinants.
source: Importantly, success in predicting the correct peptide target correlates with structural accuracy of the models, suggesting that when the pipeline succeeds, it does so by recapitulating key specificity determinants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between prediction success and structural accuracy.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer leverages inter-chain residue covariation observed in orthologs of the target proteins to identify amino acid pairs making interface contacts.
source: AlphaFold-Multimer leverages inter-chain residue covariation observed in orthologs of the target proteins to identify amino acid pairs making interface contacts.
evidence: This is a description of how AlphaFold-Multimer works, based on established knowledge of the method.

claim: TCR:pMHC interactions are determined in part by highly variable, non-germline encoded CDR3 regions.
source: Given that TCR:pMHC interactions are determined in part by highly variable, non-germline encoded CDR3 regions, it was unclear whether AlphaFold's strong docking performance on other systems would translate to TCR:pMHC interactions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about TCR biology.

claim: The AlphaFold-Multimer developers noted that it does not perform well on antibody:antigen complexes.
source: Indeed, the AlphaFold-Multimer developers noted that it does not perform well on antibody:antigen complexes, which share many features with TCR:pMHC complexes.
evidence: This claim is based on information from the AlphaFold-Multimer developers.

claim: Antibody:antigen complexes share many features with TCR:pMHC complexes.
source: Indeed, the AlphaFold-Multimer developers noted that it does not perform well on antibody:antigen complexes, which share many features with TCR:pMHC complexes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of immunological systems.

claim: Both AlphaFold-Multimer versions (AFM_full and AFM_trim) were capable of generating high-quality predictions on a nonredundant set of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes as indicated by CDR loop RMSDs at and below ~2 Å.
source: Although both models were capable of generating high-quality predictions on a nonredundant set of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes (as indicated by CDR loop RMSDs at and below ~2 Å; details below), prediction quality was highly variable, and visual inspection revealed that many of the predicted models had displaced peptides and/or TCR:pMHC docking modes that were outside the range observed in native proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prediction quality of AlphaFold-Multimer was highly variable.
source: Although both models were capable of generating high-quality predictions on a nonredundant set of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes (as indicated by CDR loop RMSDs at and below ~2 Å; details below), prediction quality was highly variable, and visual inspection revealed that many of the predicted models had displaced peptides and/or TCR:pMHC docking modes that were outside the range observed in native proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and visual inspection.

claim: Many AlphaFold-Multimer predicted models had displaced peptides and/or TCR:pMHC docking modes that were outside the range observed in native proteins.
source: Although both models were capable of generating high-quality predictions on a nonredundant set of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes (as indicated by CDR loop RMSDs at and below ~2 Å; details below), prediction quality was highly variable, and visual inspection revealed that many of the predicted models had displaced peptides and/or TCR:pMHC docking modes that were outside the range observed in native proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of the models.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer predictions took multiple hours per target to complete, limiting their throughput.
source: Additionally, these AlphaFold predictions took multiple hours per target to complete, limiting their throughput.
evidence: This is an observation about computational performance.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer does not support multi-chain templates.
source: One limitation of AlphaFold-Multimer is that it does not support multi-chain templates (Evans et al., 2021): template information from the database of solved structures can inform the internal conformation of individual chains, but it does not guide the docking of chains into higher order complexes.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of AlphaFold-Multimer, supported by a citation.

claim: In AlphaFold-Multimer, template information from the database of solved structures can inform the internal conformation of individual chains, but it does not guide the docking of chains into higher order complexes.
source: One limitation of AlphaFold-Multimer is that it does not support multi-chain templates (Evans et al., 2021): template information from the database of solved structures can inform the internal conformation of individual chains, but it does not guide the docking of chains into higher order complexes.
evidence: This is a description of how AlphaFold-Multimer uses template information, supported by a citation.

claim: The constrained nature of the TCR:pMHC binding mode suggests that higher and more consistent prediction accuracy could be obtained by providing additional template information.
source: The constrained nature of the TCR:pMHC binding mode suggests that higher and more consistent prediction accuracy could be obtained by providing additional template information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the characteristics of TCR:pMHC binding.

claim: The V-alpha and V-beta genes largely determine the best structural template for TCRs.
source: A challenge when modeling TCR structures is that the V-alpha and V-beta genes largely determine the best structural template, and these genes associate freely rather than in fixed pairings, which means that the optimal structural template for the TCR-alpha chain will often come from a different PDB structure as that for the TCR-beta chain.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of TCR biology and structure.

claim: V-alpha and V-beta genes associate freely rather than in fixed pairings.
source: A challenge when modeling TCR structures is that the V-alpha and V-beta genes largely determine the best structural template, and these genes associate freely rather than in fixed pairings, which means that the optimal structural template for the TCR-alpha chain will often come from a different PDB structure as that for the TCR-beta chain.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of TCR biology.

claim: The optimal structural template for the TCR-alpha chain will often come from a different PDB structure as that for the TCR-beta chain.
source: A challenge when modeling TCR structures is that the V-alpha and V-beta genes largely determine the best structural template, and these genes associate freely rather than in fixed pairings, which means that the optimal structural template for the TCR-alpha chain will often come from a different PDB structure as that for the TCR-beta chain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the free association of V genes.

claim: The TCR:pMHC docking mode varies widely within an overall diagonal binding mode, in a way that is not easily predicted directly from sequence.
source: Additionally, the TCR:pMHC docking mode varies widely within an overall diagonal binding mode, in a way that is not easily predicted directly from sequence, making it challenging to select an optimal template for the TCR:pMHC relative orientation.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of TCR:pMHC structural diversity.

claim: The AlphaFold-based TCR docking pipeline uses hybrid structural templates to provide a broad, native-like sampling of potential docking modes.
source: Guided by these considerations, we developed an AlphaFold-based TCR docking pipeline that uses hybrid structural templates to provide a broad, native-like sampling of potential docking modes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in this study, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Individual chain templates are first selected based on sequence similarity to the target TCR:pMHC.
source: In this approach, individual chain templates are first selected based on sequence similarity to the target TCR:pMHC (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the method, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hybrid complexes are created from individual chain templates by using a diverse set of representative docking geometries to orient the TCR chains relative to the pMHC.
source: Hybrid complexes are created from these individual chain templates by using a diverse set of representative docking geometries to orient the TCR chains relative to the pMHC (see Methods).
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in this study.

claim: Hybrid complexes are provided as templates to multiple independent AlphaFold simulations, four templates per simulation, with the highest confidence model from the simulations taken as the final prediction.
source: These hybrid complexes are provided as templates to multiple independent AlphaFold simulations, four templates per simulation, with the highest confidence model from the simulations taken as the final prediction (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the method, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: During benchmarking, templates and docking geometries from structures with similar TCRs or pMHCs to the target are excluded to reduce bias toward the native structure.
source: During benchmarking, templates and docking geometries from structures with similar TCRs or pMHCs to the target are excluded to reduce bias toward the native structure (see Methods; this constraint was not applied to the default AlphaFold-Multimer methods).
evidence: This is a description of the benchmarking methodology.

claim: The pipeline does not include additional multiple sequence alignment (MSA) information beyond the target sequence.
source: Given that we are providing template information that constrains the inter-chain docking, we chose not to include additional multiple sequence alignment (MSA) information beyond the target sequence.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice.

claim: Not including MSA information greatly speeds the predictions because MSA building is the most time-consuming part of the AlphaFold pipeline, and the neural network inference step is also significantly faster without MSA information.
source: This greatly speeds the predictions: MSA building is the most time-consuming part of the AlphaFold pipeline, and the neural network inference step is also significantly faster without MSA information.
evidence: This is an observation about computational performance based on the method design.

claim: The hybrid templates AlphaFold pipeline specialized for TCR:pMHC ('AF_TCR') produces higher quality models than either of the Alphafold-Multimer variants on a benchmark set of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes.
source: We found that the hybrid templates AlphaFold pipeline specialized for TCR:pMHC ('AF_TCR') produces higher quality models than either of the Alphafold-Multimer variants on a benchmark set (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) of 130 TCR:pMHC complexes (Figure 2A, Wilcoxon P<10–7 vs AFM_full and P<10–12 vs AFM_trim on the full set; Figure 2B, P<10–3 for both comparisons on 20 targets without a close homolog in the AlphaFold-Multimer training set; and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for peptide modeling accuracy).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 with statistical significance values.

claim: The AF_TCR pipeline outperforms the state of the art TCRpMHCmodels pipeline for Class I MHC TCR modeling.
source: The AF_TCR pipeline also outperforms the state of the art TCRpMHCmodels pipeline (Jensen et al., 2019) for Class I MHC TCR modeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B), and produces better docking geometries than simply borrowing the geometry from the most sequence-similar template (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and a citation to the TCRpMHCmodels method.

claim: The AF_TCR pipeline produces better docking geometries than simply borrowing the geometry from the most sequence-similar template.
source: The AF_TCR pipeline also outperforms the state of the art TCRpMHCmodels pipeline (Jensen et al., 2019) for Class I MHC TCR modeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B), and produces better docking geometries than simply borrowing the geometry from the most sequence-similar template (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between predicted and observed model accuracy.
source: There was a significant positive correlation between predicted and observed model accuracy (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: For 30% of the targets, the AlphaFold TCR final model had a lower RMSD than the best template docking geometry.
source: For 30% of the targets, the AlphaFold TCR final model had a lower RMSD than the best template docking geometry (Figure 2D); the final model improved over the median template RMSD for 94% of the targets (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The final AlphaFold TCR model improved over the median template RMSD for 94% of the targets.
source: For 30% of the targets, the AlphaFold TCR final model had a lower RMSD than the best template docking geometry (Figure 2D); the final model improved over the median template RMSD for 94% of the targets (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Two dominant factors contributing to docking prediction accuracy are the degree to which the docking geometry in the native structure deviates from the consensus binding mode and the MHC class.
source: We analyzed the factors contributing to docking prediction accuracy and found that two dominant factors are the degree to which the docking geometry in the native structure deviates from the consensus binding mode (as captured in a multidimensional Z score, see methods) and the MHC class (class II binding modes were better predicted than class I), with minor contributions from V gene template sequence distance, CDR loop modeling accuracy, peptide modeling accuracy, and TCRalpha/TCRbeta docking accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Class II binding modes were better predicted than class I.
source: We analyzed the factors contributing to docking prediction accuracy and found that two dominant factors are the degree to which the docking geometry in the native structure deviates from the consensus binding mode (as captured in a multidimensional Z score, see methods) and the MHC class (class II binding modes were better predicted than class I), with minor contributions from V gene template sequence distance, CDR loop modeling accuracy, peptide modeling accuracy, and TCRalpha/TCRbeta docking accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The fine-tuned AlphaFold model showed improved performance on mouse targets compared to the non-fine-tuned model.
source: We fine-tuned the AlphaFold parameters in the context of the AlphaFold TCR pipeline on the set of 93 human TCR:pMHC complexes from the benchmarking set and subsequently evaluated the performance of this model on the 37 mouse TCR:pMHC targets. Despite the small size of the TCR:pMHC ternary structure database, the fine-tuned model showed improved performance on the mouse targets (Figure 2F; Wilcoxon p<0.015), which are distinct in the details of their epitope, MHC, and TCR sequences from the human training set, suggesting that the model was able to learn generalizable features of TCR:pMHC interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F with statistical significance.

claim: The fine-tuned model was able to learn generalizable features of TCR:pMHC interactions.
source: Despite the small size of the TCR:pMHC ternary structure database, the fine-tuned model showed improved performance on the mouse targets (Figure 2F; Wilcoxon p<0.015), which are distinct in the details of their epitope, MHC, and TCR sequences from the human training set, suggesting that the model was able to learn generalizable features of TCR:pMHC interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved performance on mouse targets after training on human targets.

claim: The general problem of predicting, de novo, which peptide:MHCs a given TCR recognizes is likely to be very difficult due to the diversity of TCR:pMHC recognition modes, the polyspecificity of individual TCRs, and the paucity of available training data.
source: The general problem of predicting, de novo, which peptide:MHCs a given TCR recognizes is likely to be very difficult due to the diversity of TCR:pMHC recognition modes, the polyspecificity of individual TCRs, and the paucity of available training data (Moris et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of the problem, supported by a citation.

claim: Eight Class I peptide:MHC systems were selected for which a repertoire of paired epitope-specific TCRs and a solved ternary structure were available.
source: We selected a set of 8 Class I peptide:MHC systems (Table 1) for which a repertoire of paired epitope-specific TCRs and a solved ternary structure were available.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark dataset.

claim: These systems include one human (A*0201) and one mouse (H2-Db) MHC allele, each with 9- and 10-residue peptides.
source: These systems include one human (A*0201) and one mouse (H2-Db) MHC allele, each with 9- and 10-residue peptides.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark dataset.

claim: TCR repertoires containing more than 50 unique TCR sequences were subsampled to a set of 50 TCRs using an algorithm that removed redundancy while concentrating on the more densely sampled regions of TCR space.
source: TCR repertoires containing more than 50 unique TCR sequences were subsampled to a set of 50 TCRs using an algorithm that removed redundancy while concentrating on the more densely sampled regions of TCR space (see Methods).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: NetMHCpan-4.1 was used to select 9 decoy peptides with binding scores in the range of the true peptide binders for each MHC/peptide length combination.
source: For each MHC/peptide length combination, we used the NetMHCpan-4.1 (Reynisson et al., 2020) method to select 9 decoy peptides with binding scores in the range of the true peptide binders.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for selecting decoy peptides, with a citation to the NetMHCpan method.

claim: Raw accuracy estimates showed significant TCR- and pMHC-intrinsic effects.
source: These raw accuracy estimates showed significant TCR- and pMHC-intrinsic effects (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Certain TCRs had consistently higher or lower than average predicted interface accuracies due to features such as longer CDR3 loops or usage of V genes without a close structural template.
source: Certain TCRs had consistently higher or lower than average predicted interface accuracies due to features such as longer CDR3 loops or usage of V genes without a close structural template.
evidence: This is an observation about TCR-intrinsic effects based on the data.

claim: TCR-intrinsic factors do not change the relative order of candidate peptides, but they make comparisons of binding predictions across TCRs difficult.
source: TCR-intrinsic factors do not change the relative order of candidate peptides, but they make comparisons of binding predictions across TCRs difficult; pMHC effects have the potential to change the rank ordering of candidate peptide epitopes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of TCR-intrinsic effects.

claim: pMHC effects have the potential to change the rank ordering of candidate peptide epitopes.
source: TCR-intrinsic factors do not change the relative order of candidate peptides, but they make comparisons of binding predictions across TCRs difficult; pMHC effects have the potential to change the rank ordering of candidate peptide epitopes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of pMHC-intrinsic effects.

claim: For six of the eight epitopes, the correct peptide is ranked first when averaging the binding scores of all the TCRs in the repertoire.
source: For six of the eight epitopes, the correct peptide is ranked first when we average the binding scores of all the TCRs in the repertoire (Figure 3D; Figure 4: the largest branch of the tree is dark blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3D and 4.

claim: Epitopes with more sequence-diverse repertoires (A*0201-GLC9 and A*02:01-NLV9) are more challenging to predict.
source: It also appears that the epitopes with more sequence-diverse repertoires (A*0201-GLC9 and A*02:01-NLV9) are more challenging to predict: the trees that merge completely at smaller TCRdist values (further to the left) are bluer than the other trees in Figure 4.
evidence: This is an observation based on visual inspection of Figure 4.

claim: TCRdiv repertoire sequence diversity measure correlates with binding prediction success.
source: This can be seen quantitatively by plotting the TCRdiv repertoire sequence diversity measure (Dash et al., 2017) against measures of binding prediction success (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation to the TCRdiv measure.

claim: Some epitopes, such as A*02:01-YLQ9 and A*02:01-ELA10 are predicted very well (by area under the ROC curve, AUROC ≥ 0.96).
source: If we rank the peptides by binding score and compare the recovery of true binder peptides to decoys using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, we can see that some epitopes, such as A*02:01-YLQ9 and A*02:01-ELA10 are predicted very well (by area under the ROC curve, AUROC ≥ 0.96) and some predictions are only slightly better than random (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Some predictions are only slightly better than random.
source: If we rank the peptides by binding score and compare the recovery of true binder peptides to decoys using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, we can see that some epitopes, such as A*02:01-YLQ9 and A*02:01-ELA10 are predicted very well (by area under the ROC curve, AUROC ≥ 0.96) and some predictions are only slightly better than random (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: An overall AUROC value of 0.82 was found when binding and non-binding TCR:pMHC pairs from all epitopes are ranked together.
source: We find an overall AUROC value of 0.82 when binding and non-binding TCR:pMHC pairs from all epitopes are ranked together.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the binding prediction analysis.

claim: Well-predicted epitopes such as A*02:01-YLQ9 and A*02:01-ELA10 have smaller RMSD values than other repertoires.
source: Figure 5A shows the distribution of these RMSD values across each repertoire. Well-predicted epitopes such as A*02:01-YLQ9 and A*02:01-ELA10 indeed appear to have smaller RMSD values than other repertoires.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The mouse pMHC H2Db-ASN9 is an outlier, with an RMSD distribution shifted to very high values.
source: The mouse pMHC H2Db-ASN9 is an outlier, with an RMSD distribution shifted to very high values.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data.

claim: Three ternary structures for H2Db-ASN9 represent a unique population of TRBV17+ TCRs that is distinct from the consensus repertoire modeled.
source: Examination of the three ternary structures for this pMHC revealed that they represent a unique population of TRBV17+ TCRs that is distinct from the consensus repertoire modeled here.
evidence: This is an observation based on examination of structural data.

claim: Two of the three H2Db-ASN9 TCRs bind with a reversed docking orientation.
source: Two of the three TCRs bind with a reversed docking orientation (Gras et al., 2016), and the third has a highly displaced binding footprint (Zareie et al., 2021); all three are outliers in a hierarchical clustering tree of Class I TCRs based on docking RMSD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The third H2Db-ASN9 TCR has a highly displaced binding footprint.
source: Two of the three TCRs bind with a reversed docking orientation (Gras et al., 2016), and the third has a highly displaced binding footprint (Zareie et al., 2021); all three are outliers in a hierarchical clustering tree of Class I TCRs based on docking RMSD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three H2Db-ASN9 TCRs are outliers in a hierarchical clustering tree of Class I TCRs based on docking RMSD.
source: Two of the three TCRs bind with a reversed docking orientation (Gras et al., 2016), and the third has a highly displaced binding footprint (Zareie et al., 2021); all three are outliers in a hierarchical clustering tree of Class I TCRs based on docking RMSD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Excluding H2Db:ASN9, there is a positive correlation between docking RMSD to the closest epitope structure and binding score for the correct peptide.
source: If we exclude H2Db:ASN9 and plot docking RMSD to the closest epitope structure versus binding score for the correct peptide, we see that there is a positive correlation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The TCRs for which the correct peptide is ranked first have a lower RMSD distribution than other TCRs.
source: The TCRs for which the correct peptide is ranked first have a lower RMSD distribution than other TCRs, and this RMSD distribution shifts upward as the rank of the correct peptide declines (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The RMSD distribution shifts upward as the rank of the correct peptide declines.
source: The TCRs for which the correct peptide is ranked first have a lower RMSD distribution than other TCRs, and this RMSD distribution shifts upward as the rank of the correct peptide declines (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The correct binding predictions are driven at least in part by recovery of native-like structural features.
source: These results suggest that the correct binding predictions are driven at least in part by recovery of native-like structural features (analysis of peptide backbone RMSDs shows a positive, but much weaker, correlation between binding prediction and modeling accuracy: Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between binding prediction success and structural accuracy.

claim: Analysis of peptide backbone RMSDs shows a positive, but much weaker, correlation between binding prediction and modeling accuracy.
source: These results suggest that the correct binding predictions are driven at least in part by recovery of native-like structural features (analysis of peptide backbone RMSDs shows a positive, but much weaker, correlation between binding prediction and modeling accuracy: Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of the epitope-specific repertoires show the expected preference for the native peptide at most positions, with a subset of positions showing high sensitivity.
source: From these sensitivity plots, we can see that the majority of the epitope-specific repertoires show the expected preference for the native peptide at most positions, with a subset of positions showing high sensitivity.
evidence: This is an observation based on the alanine scanning data.

claim: Highly sensitive positions in the alanine scan are largely TCR-exposed.
source: Coloring the pMHC structures by mutation sensitivity (Figure 6A) reveals that these highly sensitive positions are largely TCR-exposed; several are sites of known viral escape mutations, such as A*02:01-KLV position L5 (Wölfl et al., 2008) and H2Db-SSL position R7 (Valkenburg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Several highly sensitive positions are sites of known viral escape mutations, such as A*02:01-KLV position L5 and H2Db-SSL position R7.
source: Coloring the pMHC structures by mutation sensitivity (Figure 6A) reveals that these highly sensitive positions are largely TCR-exposed; several are sites of known viral escape mutations, such as A*02:01-KLV position L5 (Wölfl et al., 2008) and H2Db-SSL position R7 (Valkenburg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Peptide anchor mutations are not among the most strongly predicted positions in the alanine scan.
source: The fact that peptide anchor mutations are not among the most strongly predicted positions here suggests that, by subtracting each peptide's average binding score for the background 'non-binder' TCRs, we are able to correct for these peptide-intrinsic features.
